strengths: 1987 JNR privatization/split into JR groups is stated correctly and not over-explained
Tokyo Metro and Toei as two subway operators is accurate
No invented yen figures; through-running and IC-as-payment-only are the right institutional facts
verified: Japanese National Railways divided and privatized in 1987 into JR companies
Tokyo has two subway operators: Tokyo Metro and Toei
Through-running (直通運転) lets some suburban trains continue onto subway tracks
Yamanote is a JR loop, not a subway
Hankyu-associated private railways historically combined rails, housing, and a terminal department store (pattern, not universal)
Suica, Pasmo, ICOCA and similar IC cards interoperate for payment without merging companies
questionable: Crossing company boundaries 'adds a transfer fare' (sounds like a surcharge rather than stacked operator fares, sometimes with a transfer discount)
Enter JR gate / exit subway gate on a valid tap (true for many IC through-journeys, easy to misread as any gate pair)
unsupported: Staff answer with company names first as a default script

issues.location: ## How Japanese People Live Inside the Patchwork (fares)
issues.problem: 'Crossing company boundaries can add a transfer fare' is the wrong mechanism. Riders typically pay each operator’s fare (sometimes with a 乗継割引). There is not a standard extra 'transfer fee,' and inventing a yen example would be worse.
issues.suggestion: Say you often pay more than a same-distance trip on one company because two (or more) fares stack—without quoting yen.

issues.problem: JR-in / subway-out on one tap is true only for a valid connected journey. Readers may think unpaid corridors are fair game.
issues.suggestion: Keep the hedge 'depending on the journey' and add that you must follow a valid route, not wander between unpaid areas.

issues.location: ## How Japanese People Live Inside the Patchwork
issues.problem: 'The first train after 5 a.m.' is a mood detail, not a network fact; first trains vary by line.
issues.suggestion: Soften to early-morning first trains, without a clock-time that sounds official.
